overview: This label refers to Tippu Tip’s commercial and military power in eastern Congo, centred on Kasongo. Ivory trading, slavery and caravan routes linked it to Zanzibar. The imported 1878 to 1914 outline overstates its duration: colonial conquest broke this power in the 1890s, well before the map endpoint.

periods.title: Kasongo and the caravan network
periods.summary: Kasongo was a major inland market and the centre of Tippu Tip’s commercial domain.

periods.title: War and colonial conquest
periods.summary: The Congo Free State’s campaign destroyed the merchants’ political power.

periods.title: After the imported state label
periods.summary: This part of the map window belongs to the colonial aftermath, with continuing local communities.

items.text: Tippu Tip said that kinship with Kasongo’s ruler helped him gain authority in Utetera. His account traced this connection through an enslaved grandmother and presented his acceptance as voluntary. Historians treat that story critically: it is also an ambitious ruler’s explanation of why he deserved to rule.

The trading domain depended on alliances, armed followers and links with Zanzibar. Tippu Tip also accepted a position within Leopold II’s Congo Free State. Rivals could cooperate when it suited them; the later war should not hide the earlier bargains between European officials and slave-trading leaders.

Enslavement separated relatives and placed people under others’ control. Women’s family connections sometimes influenced their position in a captor’s household, but that did not make their capture voluntary. A history focused only on successful merchants misses the people whose coerced labour sustained their wealth.

Excavations in 2018 and 2019 confirmed Old Kasongo, called Tongoni, and large platforms supporting merchants’ residences. A house attributed to Tippu Tip measured about 10.9 by 6.6 metres. Archaeologists suggest that the raised platforms could also help defend the settlement.

Carved doors, lintels and windows decorated merchants’ houses, connecting inland architecture with the Swahili coast. After conquest, some fittings were reused in colonial buildings before entering museums. A surviving door can therefore tell several stories: skilled workmanship, domestic life and the dismantling of a town.

A CT scan of one carved lintel identified its wood, with some certainty, as African crabwood found in eastern Congo. The researchers suggested that coastal craftspeople may have worked with local timber. The design travelled a long way; the tree may have grown much closer to home.

After the 1893 capture, military doctor Sidney Hinde described stores of rice, maize and coffee and gardens containing oranges, guavas, mangoes and other fruit. His account shows a substantial food-producing settlement, although his admiration for prosperous estates tells us little about the workers who supplied them.

Hinde also reported carved beds with silk mosquito curtains and mattresses that soldiers seized. These were furnishings in wealthy households, not a picture of everyone’s bedroom. They reveal both long-distance access to luxury textiles and the way conquest turned someone’s belongings into another person’s loot.

Kasongo had Quran schools where children learned to read and write. Kalenda Njike, a son of the leader Ngongo Lutete, was among their pupils. A later photograph from 1904 shows children using wooden writing boards, evidence that this educational tradition continued after the merchants’ military defeat.

Writing sample: “nataka mashauri kwako” means “I want your advice.” Sayf bin Rashid wrote this Swahili phrase from Kasongo to the official Tobback on 13 May 1891. His letter used Roman letters, with an Arabic signature; here a word split across two manuscript lines is joined.

Cloth could settle a food bill. A surviving receipt dated 25 January 1892 records 410 lengths of cloth owed for rice supplied to the Stanley Falls official Tobback. Such paperwork gives a concrete glimpse of the wider trading network: textiles were payment as well as clothing.

During research meetings in Kasongo in 2021 and 2022, residents asked for protection of the old settlement and a community museum. Family memories helped explain objects kept abroad. They wanted future generations to learn this difficult history in Kasongo itself, close to the places their ancestors knew.

ending.text: Kasongo fell to Congo Free State forces in 1893, and the wider campaign ended in colonial victory in 1894. This destroyed the trading rulers’ political dominance, not the communities of Maniema or their Swahili and Islamic traditions.
